paragraphs: The paper proposes a probabilistic explanation for how making a decision can influence what someone subsequently perceives. Its starting point is that observers may consider several hypotheses about the physical process behind a sensory signal. Perception can be optimal when each hypothesis contributes according to the observer’s correct belief in it.

The key change occurs when an observer commits to one hypothesis. In the model, that commitment turns a tentative belief into subjective certainty. Subsequent estimation then uses only the selected explanation, rather than continuing to account for alternatives. This provides a mechanism through which an earlier decision can bias a later perceptual estimate.

The authors show that the model accounts well for data from a decision-followed-by-estimation experiment, including the direction of the estimation bias. Its only free parameter describes uncertainty in the observer’s internal sensory representation; the experiment determines the remaining parameters. This constrained setup also supports quantitative predictions for two modifications of the experiment. Those predictions extend the framework’s reach without requiring additional adjustable parameters.
neurips-2007-a-bayesian-model-of-conditi.tldr: A Bayesian model explains how committing to a perceptual decision can bias subsequent estimates by treating one hypothesis as certain.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning linear dynamical systems that remain stable, a property that learning algorithms often leave unenforced. The authors approximate the learning problem with a convex optimization program. They begin with a relaxed version and progressively add constraints intended to improve the stability of the learned system.

A central design choice is to test the system’s actual stability after each step. The algorithm can stop once stability is achieved, even if it has not satisfied every constraint of the approximate convex program. Because that program is only a proxy for the desired problem, enforcing all of its constraints can be unnecessarily restrictive. Early stopping can therefore produce a higher-quality solution.

The authors apply the method to dynamic textures learned from image sequences and to drug-sales data used in biosurveillance. They report noticeable improvements in simulated sequence quality. Comparisons with methods by Lacy and Bernstein are also positive for accuracy, simulation quality, and efficiency. These results support checking the desired system property directly while incrementally tightening an optimization approximation.
neurips-2007-a-constraint-generation-app.tldr: Incrementally adding constraints and stopping when stability is achieved can improve learned linear dynamical systems and their simulated sequences.

paragraphs: The paper treats the construction of a nearest-neighbor search structure as a learning problem. Instead of choosing its parameters without observing how it will be queried, the proposed framework uses sample queries as training evidence. The goal is to configure the structure so that retrieval is faster, misses are less frequent, or both objectives improve.

The authors develop this idea for two established families: KD-trees and the rectilinear structures used in locality-sensitive hashing. They provide simple learning algorithms for both families. This makes the proposal more concrete than a general suggestion to tune search systems: it identifies existing structures whose parameters can be learned from examples of their intended use.

The paper also derives generalization theory for these classes of data structures, addressing the connection between performance on sample queries and performance beyond those samples. Experiments show that learning often improves the already strong performance of the underlying structures. The qualification matters: the reported benefit is frequent improvement, not a claim that learned configurations always outperform their alternatives.
neurips-2007-a-learning-framework-for-ne.tldr: Learning search-structure parameters from sample queries often improves nearest-neighbor retrieval time or miss rate.

paragraphs: The paper studies regret in online convex optimization: how a learner’s accumulated performance compares with an appropriate retrospective choice as functions arrive over time. Its focus is the rate at which regret grows, and how that rate depends on the curvature of the functions being observed.

The first contribution extends an existing algorithm so that it no longer requires advance knowledge of a lower bound on second derivatives. This removes a particular piece of information that would otherwise need to be supplied before learning begins. The authors then introduce Adaptive Online Gradient Descent, which connects previously established results for linear functions and strongly convex functions.

The adaptive algorithm achieves intermediate regret rates between those endpoint settings, allowing the analysis to reflect a broader range of curvature behavior. The paper also establishes a strong optimality result and extends its conclusions to general norms. Together, these contributions make the regret analysis less dependent on knowing a curvature bound in advance and less restricted to a single geometric setting.
neurips-2007-adaptive-online-gradient-de.tldr: Adaptive Online Gradient Descent obtains curvature-sensitive regret rates without requiring advance knowledge of a lower curvature bound.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis aims to separate signals that have been mixed together. The paper approaches this task through a question about neural computation: what learning mechanism could allow neurons to perform such separation? The authors contrast their approach with algorithms that mainly use higher-order properties of signal amplitudes while ignoring temporal correlations.

Their proposed online rule instead exploits delayed correlations in the inputs. It detects joint changes in the firing rates of a neuron sending a signal and a neuron receiving it. The resulting update resembles a local, rate-based Hebbian learning rule, linking the signal-separation computation to activity available at a connection between neurons.

The stated contribution is that this rule performs independent component analysis using temporal information in an online learning setting. The abstract also identifies whitening, which removes second-order correlations, as preprocessing required by many existing approaches. The paper’s central explanatory shift is toward delayed relationships and local firing-rate changes as ingredients of an ICA mechanism, rather than relying solely on the distribution of instantaneous signal amplitudes.
neurips-2007-an-online-hebbian-learning-.tldr: An online learning rule performs independent component analysis by exploiting delayed input correlations and local changes in neural firing rates.

paragraphs: The paper presents a globally convergent optimization method for regularized risk minimization. This formulation combines the objective of fitting observations with a regularization term. The method applies when the resulting optimization problem is convex, providing a common framework for several learning tasks instead of requiring a separate optimization treatment for each.

The authors identify support vector estimation, regression, and Gaussian processes among the applications covered by this framework. They also show that SVMPerf is a special case. That relationship places an existing specialized approach inside a broader method and helps explain the scope of the proposed unification.

The theoretical results give tight bounds on the number of steps needed to reach a requested precision. For general convex problems, the bound grows in proportion to the inverse of that precision. For continuously differentiable problems, it grows logarithmically with the inverse precision. Thus, the stated guarantees distinguish between general convex objectives and the smoother case. Experiments demonstrate the method’s performance alongside this convergence analysis.
neurips-2007-bundle-methods-for-machine-.tldr: A unified method for convex regularized risk minimization provides global convergence and stronger iteration bounds for continuously differentiable objectives.

paragraphs: The paper examines a tension between statistical consistency and convergence speed in model selection and prediction. Bayesian model averaging, Bayesian model selection, and approximations such as BIC are generally consistent, yet can converge more slowly than AIC or leave-one-out cross-validation. Those faster alternatives, however, can be inconsistent.

The authors identify a catch-up phenomenon as an explanation for slow convergence in Bayesian methods. They use this analysis to construct the switch-distribution, a modification of the distribution used in Bayesian model averaging. The proposed change therefore targets a diagnosed source of slow learning rather than simply choosing one side of the consistency-versus-speed comparison.

The paper proves that selection and prediction based on the switch-distribution are both consistent and achieve optimal convergence rates in many situations. The scope of that result matters: it is not presented as an unconditional guarantee for every setting. An efficient algorithm makes the proposal practical as well as theoretical. The contribution is a route to combining two desirable properties that the compared methods do not always deliver together.
neurips-2007-catching-up-faster-in-bayes.tldr: The switch-distribution modifies Bayesian model averaging to achieve both consistency and optimal convergence rates in many situations.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to incorporate invariances into a learning algorithm. An invariance expresses that certain changes in an input should preserve the relevant prediction. The optimization challenge is to encode that requirement while retaining a formulation that can be handled by existing learning machinery.

The authors provide a convex formulation and state that it can accommodate arbitrary loss functions. Their approach relies on column generation rather than directly modifying the underlying optimization problem. This choice is central to the contribution: the mechanism for introducing invariance is designed to work with optimization machinery that is already available.

The formulation is presented as a drop-in replacement for most kernel optimization algorithms, including solvers in the SVMStruct family. Its stated value is therefore both mathematical and practical: it offers a convex treatment of invariance while maintaining broad compatibility with established solvers. The abstract emphasizes formulation and integration, making the contribution a general way to bring invariance requirements into learning systems across different choices of loss.
neurips-2007-convex-learning-with-invari.tldr: A convex, column-generation formulation incorporates invariances while remaining compatible with most kernel optimization solvers.

paragraphs: DIFFRAC frames clustering through a linear discriminative cost: the proposed partition is evaluated using a criterion concerned with distinguishing its groups. The underlying assignment problem is combinatorial, so the authors replace it with a convex relaxation. They solve the resulting large optimization problem through a sequence of smaller singular value decompositions.

The framework also supports two extensions. A discriminative cost based on positive definite kernels allows nonlinear clustering, positioning the method as an alternative to spectral clustering. Prior information about the partition can also be incorporated, allowing the same framework to address semi-supervised clustering or classification.

Experiments on synthetic and real medium-scale datasets report better clustering performance than K-means, particularly in robustness to noise. With prior information, the authors report state-of-the-art semi-supervised performance. These are empirical findings for the evaluated settings. The broader contribution is a flexible optimization framework that connects unsupervised grouping, nonlinear separation, and partial supervision through changes to the cost or information supplied to the partitioning problem.
neurips-2007-diffrac-a-discriminative-an.tldr: DIFFRAC uses a convex relaxation of discriminative clustering and supports kernels and prior partition information, with strong reported empirical performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning the structure of junction trees with bounded treewidth. These probabilistic models are attractive because they can represent distributions compactly while allowing efficient exact inference. The challenge is to learn such a structure from observations without losing those computational advantages during the learning process itself.

The authors present what they describe as the first truly polynomial algorithm for this task. When treewidth is held constant, both running time and sample requirements are polynomial. The analysis also gives guarantees expressed through KL divergence, a measure of discrepancy between the learned distribution and the true one. The constant-treewidth qualification is central to these complexity claims.

A key theoretical ingredient bounds conditional mutual information for arbitrarily large variable sets using only polynomially many mutual-information computations on fixed-size subsets. This applies when the underlying distribution can be approximated by a bounded-treewidth junction tree. A lazy extension produces substantial practical speedups, and evaluations on several real datasets demonstrate that the overall learning approach is viable in practice.
neurips-2007-efficient-principled-learni.tldr: For constant treewidth, the paper gives polynomial-time, polynomial-sample junction-tree structure learning with distributional guarantees and practical speedups.

paragraphs: Ensemble clustering combines several proposed clusterings into one consolidated partition. The paper asks how to preserve the information shared across those inputs. The authors argue that an agreement measure based on a two-dimensional string encoding captures this relationship better than the voting-based strategies previously used for aggregation.

They first express maximization of the new agreement measure as a nonlinear optimization problem. Through convexification techniques, they transform it into an exact binary semidefinite program. They then relax the binary formulation to obtain a semidefinite program that can be solved in polynomial time. The efficient solvability claim applies to the relaxed problem, preserving the distinction between the original discrete formulation and its tractable replacement.

Evaluations use clustering and image-segmentation databases. The experiments indicate improvements under both the newly proposed measure and existing voting-based agreement measures. This is significant because the reported gains are not confined to the criterion introduced by the authors. The paper contributes both an alternative definition of agreement and an optimization route for using it.
neurips-2007-ensemble-clustering-using-s.tldr: A new clustering-agreement measure and semidefinite relaxation improve ensemble aggregation under both new and existing evaluation criteria in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper targets a practical imbalance in activity recognition: sensor traces are relatively easy to collect, but assigning labels to them is expensive and tedious. It also addresses feature selection, since retaining a small set of informative features can help both computational speed and predictive accuracy.

The proposed semi-supervised virtual evidence boosting algorithm extends virtual evidence boosting for conditional random fields. It performs parameter estimation and feature selection while using both labeled and unlabeled examples. Its objective combines conditional pseudo-likelihood on labeled data with conditional entropy on unlabeled data. Minimum entropy regularization gives the unlabeled traces a role in training by favoring more confident conditional predictions.

Experiments on synthetic data and activity traces from wearable sensors show benefits from both unlabeled data and automatic feature selection. The method also outperforms the other semi-supervised training approaches considered in those experiments. The authors report reductions in overall system cost and human labeling cost, connecting the training formulation to two concrete burdens involved in building activity-recognition systems.
neurips-2007-fast-and-scalable-training-.tldr: Semi-supervised virtual evidence boosting trains CRFs with unlabeled data and automatic feature selection, reducing costs and improving tested activity-recognition performance.

paragraphs: FilterBoost studies boosting in a filtering setting, where the learner requests examples from an oracle instead of repeatedly working with a fixed training set. This access pattern offers a way to train efficiently when datasets are very large. The proposed algorithm builds on a logistic-regression technique introduced by Collins, Schapire, and Singer.

The theoretical contribution is to obtain bounds matching or improving earlier work while requiring fewer assumptions. The authors also give the first proof that the Collins and colleagues algorithm is a strong PAC learner within the filtering setting. That qualification is essential: the proof establishes the learning guarantee for this particular mode of obtaining examples.

The analysis addresses both classification and estimation of conditional probabilities, and extensive experiments support the theoretical results. In probability estimation, the algorithm is empirically more robust to noise and overfitting than batch boosters. For classification, its performance is competitive. These distinct conclusions matter because good probability estimates and accurate class decisions are related objectives, but the reported comparative advantages are different.
neurips-2007-filterboost-regression-and-.tldr: FilterBoost combines filtering-based boosting guarantees with improved empirical robustness in probability estimation and competitive classification performance.

paragraphs: The paper argues that theories of behavioral control should give episodic memory a larger role. It starts from accounts featuring two controllers: one associated with a forward model and prefrontal cortex, and another using computationally simpler habitual actor-critic methods associated with part of the striatum.

The proposed third controller is associated with episodic memory, the hippocampus, and medial temporal cortices. The authors offer a normative argument, asking under what circumstances this form of control should be useful. Their analysis examines a class of simple environments to identify situations in which relying on episodic control would make sense.

The results support its usefulness across cases involving complexity and noisy inference, especially early in learning before habitual behavior has developed. This gives episodic control a particular role within a broader system of controllers, rather than treating it as a universal replacement. The authors also interpret evidence of control transferring from the hippocampus to the striatum through this hypothesis, connecting the theoretical argument to observed changes in neural involvement.
neurips-2007-hippocampal-contributions-t.tldr: The paper argues that episodic memory provides a useful third form of control, particularly early in learning under complexity and inferential noise.

paragraphs: The paper investigates when support vector machines can estimate conditional quantiles, including the median. A conditional quantile describes a position within the outcome distribution for a given input. The analysis compares two loss functions, pinball loss and epsilon-insensitive loss, to clarify what their use actually guarantees about the quantity being estimated.

For pinball loss, the authors give a condition on the data-generating distribution that ensures approximation of conditional quantiles in the L1 sense. This specifies a distributional setting in which the loss supports the desired estimation target. They then use that result to derive an oracle inequality for a support vector machine trained with pinball loss.

For epsilon-insensitive loss, the conclusion is more restrictive: the resulting support vector machine estimates the conditional median only under certain conditions on the distribution. The distinction matters when interpreting a regression output. The paper ties the meaning of the estimated quantity to both the chosen loss and properties of the data-generating process, rather than assigning a median interpretation automatically.
neurips-2007-how-svms-can-estimate-quant.tldr: The paper establishes distribution-dependent guarantees for SVM quantile estimation and shows that epsilon-insensitive regression estimates the median only under certain conditions.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how elapsed time might be inferred from neural activity that is structured but random. Timing matters for processes such as speech recognition, movement, and learning, yet the mechanisms behind temporal judgments remain uncertain. Existing proposed mechanisms often rely on a state whose evolution is temporally predictable, such as an oscillation or a decaying memory trace.

The alternative explored here is that observations of a stochastic process could provide evidence about elapsed time. Randomness does not eliminate temporal structure: typical neural and sensory processes contain statistical relationships across multiple timescales. Such processes therefore need not be dedicated exclusively to timing to become candidates for temporal estimation.

The authors investigate the statistical properties of an elapsed-time estimator built from a simple family of stochastic processes. The contribution is an analysis of this alternative basis for timing, framed as a possible mechanism rather than an established account of human temporal judgments. It shifts the question toward how statistical structure in ongoing activity might carry information about the passage of time.
neurips-2007-inferring-elapsed-time-from.tldr: The paper studies whether elapsed time can be estimated from the statistical structure of stochastic processes rather than a predictably evolving internal state.

paragraphs: Natural sounds contain meaningful structure at very different timescales. In speech, broad sentence structure coexists with much shorter phonemes, glottal pulses, and formants. The paper argues that understanding auditory processing benefits from algorithms that can use this range of structure, since the auditory system draws on information across these scales.

The authors identify two obstacles to doing so computationally. Combining short and long temporal information is technically difficult, and processing long recordings at sufficiently fine resolution is expensive. These pressures help explain why machine-audition algorithms have concentrated largely on shorter structures while leaving longer ones underused.

The contribution is a statistical model for natural sounds that captures structure across a wide range of timescales, together with efficient learning and inference algorithms. The authors demonstrate the approach on a missing-data task. This provides evidence that the model’s representation can be useful for reasoning about incomplete sounds, while the efficient algorithms address the computational difficulty that motivates the work. The stated demonstration concerns that task rather than every auditory-processing problem.
neurips-2007-modeling-natural-sounds-wit.tldr: A statistical sound model captures structure across multiple timescales with efficient learning and inference, demonstrated on a missing-data task.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an AND/OR graph for representing the different configurations of deformable, articulated objects such as horses. Its representation uses a summarization principle: lower-level nodes pass summary statistics upward. This organizes information across the graph without requiring higher-level nodes to receive every detail from below.

The model’s probability distributions are invariant to position, orientation, and scale. Inference combines two directions of processing. A bottom-up stage proposes possible horse configurations, while a top-down stage refines and validates them. This connects local evidence with a broader interpretation of the object’s configuration.

The authors also apply surround suppression to ensure that inference time is polynomial in the size of the input. They evaluate the algorithm on detecting horses, segmenting them from images, and parsing their structure. The reported results show fast inference and performance comparable with state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution therefore joins a representation for variable object configurations with an inference procedure designed to keep the search computationally manageable across these related tasks.
neurips-2007-rapid-inference-on-a-novel-.tldr: An AND/OR graph combines bottom-up proposals and top-down refinement for fast horse detection, segmentation, and parsing with polynomial inference time.

paragraphs: The paper develops a regret-minimization technique for solving large extensive games with incomplete information. Such games describe decisions made over time when players do not know everything relevant to the situation. Finding a Nash equilibrium becomes computationally demanding as the number of possible game states grows.

The central contribution is counterfactual regret, a quantity designed to exploit the game’s incomplete-information structure. The authors show that minimizing this quantity also minimizes overall regret. This connection makes counterfactual regret useful for equilibrium computation: through self-play, the technique can be used to compute a Nash equilibrium.

The practical demonstration concerns poker. The method solves abstractions of limit Texas Hold’em containing as many as one trillion states, a scale two orders of magnitude larger than previous methods. The fact that these are abstractions matters: the reported achievement concerns those game representations. Together, the regret connection and the poker demonstration show how a theoretically motivated objective can support equilibrium computation at substantially larger scales.
neurips-2007-regret-minimization-in-game.tldr: Counterfactual regret links incomplete-information game structure to regret minimization, enabling self-play equilibrium computation for much larger poker abstractions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a resource-constrained radar network should adapt its scanning as weather phenomena evolve. The radars can scan selected sectors, creating a decision about where to direct sensing effort. The authors compare three strategies that differ in how much predicted future information they use.

The sit-and-spin strategy repeatedly scans the full circle. Limited lookahead also considers the environmental state predicted a specified number of decision steps ahead using Kalman filters. Full lookahead represents the problem as a Markov decision process and uses reinforcement learning to estimate an optimal scanning strategy based on expected future states.

The results identify circumstances in which lookahead is most beneficial: multiple weather phenomena are present, and their maximum radius is sufficiently smaller than the radars’ radius. The authors also find a tradeoff between average scanning quality and the delay before a phenomenon is scanned again. This means scan planning must balance the quality of observations against revisit frequency; the reported benefits of prediction depend on the environment’s structure.
neurips-2007-scan-strategies-for-meteoro.tldr: Predictive radar scanning is most beneficial for multiple sufficiently small weather phenomena, with a tradeoff between observation quality and revisit delay.

paragraphs: The paper examines an alternative representation for dynamic programming and reinforcement learning. The authors’ previously introduced approach explicitly maintains stationary distributions in place of value functions. This changes the central object tracked by the algorithm: its representation concerns stationary behavior rather than a function assigning values.

Here, the authors focus on the convergence properties of these dual algorithms. They investigate those properties through both theoretical analysis and empirical study. Convergence is a central question for such a representational change because introducing a different quantity to maintain also raises the question of how the resulting iterative learning procedure behaves.

The paper additionally shows how function approximation can be incorporated to scale up the approach. This connects the investigation of convergence with the practical issue of using the representation in larger problems. The stated contribution is therefore a study of the behavior and scalability of an existing dual approach, combining mathematical and empirical examination with an approximation-based extension. Its significance lies in developing stationary-distribution methods as an alternative foundation for these learning and planning algorithms.
neurips-2007-stable-dual-dynamic-program.tldr: The paper studies convergence and function-approximation-based scaling for dynamic programming algorithms that maintain stationary distributions instead of value functions.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a distribution for a binary output conditioned on several binary inputs. It builds the representation from noisy-or and noisy-and-not combinations of causal features, where each feature is a conjunction of inputs. This allows combinations of inputs to participate in the model’s logical structure.

Standard noisy-or and noisy-and-not models are special cases of this broader distribution. The authors prove a completeness result: with sufficiently many causal factors, the representation can express every conditional distribution of the specified binary form. The qualification about the number of factors is essential. The result establishes representational coverage when enough factors are available.

The authors illustrate the model by showing that it can account for experimental findings about human causal reasoning in more complex contexts. This connects the representational proposal to observed reasoning behavior without establishing it as the unique explanation of that behavior. The paper also speculates about broader uses in causal reasoning and artificial intelligence, distinguishing those possible applications from its proof of completeness and its experimental illustration.
neurips-2007-the-noisy-logical-distribut.tldr: The noisy-logical distribution generalizes familiar causal models and can represent any binary conditional distribution given sufficiently many causal factors.

paragraphs: The paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding learning when optimization is approximate. Rather than treating the learning objective as if it were solved exactly, the analysis includes the effect of the optimization procedure. This makes the computation used to obtain a model part of the account of learning performance.

For small-scale problems, the analysis retains the familiar tradeoff between approximation and estimation. These terms distinguish how well a chosen model can represent the target from how well it can be learned from available observations. The paper identifies this as the usual balance governing the smaller-scale setting.

For large-scale problems, the tradeoff changes qualitatively: the computational complexity of the optimization algorithm enters in nontrivial ways. Consequently, the analysis of a learning method must account for how its solution is computed, alongside its approximation and estimation properties. The contribution is a framework that separates these regimes and explains why conclusions based on the usual small-scale tradeoff need not transfer directly when learning operates at a larger scale.
neurips-2007-the-tradeoffs-of-large-scal.tldr: Accounting for approximate optimization reveals that large-scale learning involves computational tradeoffs beyond the usual approximation–estimation balance.

paragraphs: The paper combines offline approximation with online search for planning under partial observability. Offline methods provide theoretical guarantees, while online methods have shown strong scalability. The authors seek to retain both advantages by using search at decision time to reduce errors in an approximate value function computed beforehand.

Their anytime algorithm directs search using heuristics derived from an analysis of lookahead error. These heuristics prioritize reachable beliefs with the greatest potential to reduce error. A belief represents uncertainty about the environment, so this strategy focuses computation on possible information states relevant to the current planning problem.

The authors prove a general theorem establishing that the heuristics are admissible and lead to complete, epsilon-optimal algorithms. The epsilon qualification means the target is a specified tolerance from optimality. Empirical evidence also shows that the approach can find provably near-optimal solutions in reasonable time. The contribution links practical search guidance to formal error guarantees, making online refinement part of a theoretically supported planning procedure.
neurips-2007-theoretical-analysis-of-heu.tldr: Error-guided online search refines offline POMDP approximations with completeness and epsilon-optimality guarantees, supported by practical empirical results.

paragraphs: The paper studies product recommendation based on users’ preferences for the visual content of images. It identifies two connected modeling choices: which visual features are relevant and how many classes the model should use. Both choices matter when images are represented by many continuous descriptors.

The authors propose a generative model with separate class structure for users and visual features. They use a message-length approach to select relevant features while identifying the numbers of user and image classes. Treating these decisions together lets feature selection and model size be determined within the same modeling procedure.

The target is accurate rating prediction for multidimensional image descriptors whose distributions need not be Gaussian. Experiments on collected data demonstrate merits of the proposed approach. The stated evidence supports the combined modeling strategy in that evaluated setting. Its broader methodological contribution is to make visual relevance and class structure joint parts of recommendation learning, rather than treating the feature set and number of groups as independently fixed inputs.
neurips-2007-unsupervised-feature-select.tldr: A generative recommendation model jointly selects visual features and class counts using message length, with supportive results on collected image-rating data.
